bib.title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v6, 19 Oct 2025; first posted Nov 2024)

read.skipped: Reference list (chars 184821 to end) only skimmed for arXiv ids; everything before it read line by line.

question: How can reliable LLM-as-a-Judge systems be built, improved and evaluated?
hypothesis: Stronger reasoning and instruction-following backbones, plus aggregation and prompt strategies, make judges more reliable; the survey also expects reasoning models to be better judges.
contributions: Formal and informal definition of LLM-as-a-Judge, plus a contextualised definition of reliability
A unified framework mapping the literature to four questions: what it is, how to use it, how to improve it, how to evaluate it
Comparative analyses and a meta-evaluation experiment on judge models and improvement strategies
Applications, challenges and a future-work agenda

method.summary: Literature survey organised around the judge pipeline E <- P_LLM(x (+) C): in-context prompt design, model selection, post-processing, evaluation pipeline. Section 4.4 adds the survey's own small meta-evaluation: 6 plus 4 reasoning LLMs as pairwise judges on LLMEval2 (agreement) and EvalBiasBench plus swapped-position pairs (bias), and four improvement strategies applied to GPT-3.5-turbo.
method.task: meta-evaluation of LLM judges (pairwise preference agreement with humans, bias accuracy, position consistency)

other.note: base evaluator for the strategy comparison in Table 4
reasoning judges, evaluated on Table 2 and Table 3 only; versions and settings not given

inference.prompting: Judge prompt text for the experiment is not given

metrics.name: Accuracy (bias)
metrics.definition: proportion of EvalBiasBench samples where the judge picks the correct (unbiased) response

metrics.name: Position Consistency
metrics.definition: share of N samples where the judge picks the same response after swapping response positions: sum I(S_r12 = S_r21) / N (outputs r1, r2 or TIE)

baselines: GPT-3.5-turbo base evaluator vs each strategy (Table 4)
eval.protocol: Single run per cell, temperature 0; no seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests reported.

availability.data: Resource site https://awesome-llm-as-a-judge.github.io/ (stated in abstract); code for the meta-evaluation tool (Fig 13) not linked in text

prompts.purpose: Likert-scale scoring example (from Gao et al.)
prompts.text: Evaluate the quality of summaries written for a news article. Rate each summary on four dimensions: {Dimension_1}, {Dimension_2}, {Dimension_3}, and {Dimension_4}. You should rate on a scale from 1 (worst) to 5 (best). Article: {Article} Summary: {Summary}

prompts.purpose: Pairwise comparison example (from Gao et al.)
prompts.text: Given a new article, which summary is better? Answer "Summary 0" or "Summary 1". You do not need to explain the reason. Article: {Article} Summary 0: {Summary_0} Summary 1: {Summary_1}
Is the sentence supported by the article? Answer "Yes" or "No". Article: {Article} Sentence: {Sentence}

evidence.quote: we set the hyper-parameter temperature to 0 to reduce the impact of randomness in LLMs’ output

results.claim: Judge models differ little in agreement with human labels on LLMEval2; GPT-4-turbo reaches only 61.54% (percentage agreement).
results.setup: LLMEval2, 2,553 samples with swapped positions (n=5106), pairwise judging, temperature 0, GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09; baseline is GPT-3.5-turbo
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-4-turbo, column Alignment with Human
results.note: Survey text says no significant alignment differences between LLMs and clear room for improvement.

results.claim: GPT-4-turbo has the highest position consistency among the six standard LLMs (80.31%); GPT-3.5-turbo 68.78%, LLaMA3-8B 38.85%.
results.setup: swapped-position pairs from LLMEval2 and EvalBiasBench, temperature 0
results.note: Reasoning judges: gemini-2.0-thinking 76.84, o1-mini 76.73, o3-mini 74.63, deepseek r1 69.17.

results.claim: Length bias accuracy is poor for all non-GPT-4 judges (GPT-3.5-turbo 20.59%, LLaMA3-8B 20.59%, Mistral-7B 26.47%) while GPT-4-turbo gets 91.18%.
results.setup: EvalBiasBench length-bias subset, n=34; value is GPT-3.5-turbo, baseline is GPT-4-turbo
results.note: Survey prose: 'apart from Concreteness Bias and Content Continuation Bias, the performance of LLMs, except GPT-4-turbo, was generally poor, particularly in the Length Bias.'

results.claim: Even GPT-4-turbo degrades on Empty Reference (65.38%) and Nested Instruction (70.83%) biases.
results.setup: EvalBiasBench empty-reference subset, n=26, GPT-4-turbo; nested instruction n=24 gives 70.83
results.quote: Even GPT-4-turbo experienced substantial degradation in Empty Reference Bias and Nested Instruction Bias.
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-4-turbo, columns Empty Reference and Nested Instruction

results.claim: Asking for an explanation with the verdict (w/ explanation) lowers GPT-3.5-turbo position consistency from 68.78% to 48.97% and agreement from 54.72% to 52.47%.
results.setup: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 base evaluator, temperature 0, LLMEval2 and EvalBiasBench
results.quote: However, in terms of evaluation performance and bias mitigation, it generally has a negative impact.
results.table: Table 4, row w/ explanation, column Position
results.note: Survey speculates the drop is from deeper biases introduced by self-explanation; the cause is not tested.

results.quote: Self Validation (w/ self-validation) shows minimal effectiveness, likely due to the LLMs’ overconfidence, which may limit its re-evaluation efforts during self-validation.
results.table: Table 4, row w/ self-validation, column Alignment with Human

results.claim: Majority vote over 5 rounds is the multi-round variant that helps (position consistency 70.11% vs 68.78%); mean@5 (69.58) and best-of-5 (58.72) do not help, and best-of-5 lowers agreement to 51.95%.
results.note: Table 4 majority@5 Position cell is printed '70 11' in the text layer (decimal point lost), so the number is not machine-checkable; read as 70.11. mean@5 69.58, best-of-5 58.72, base 68.78. majority@5 length accuracy 26.47 vs 20.59 base.

results.claim: Multi-LLM voting is sensitive to which models are in the panel: swapping LLaMA3-8B for Qwen2.5-7B lifts position consistency from 32.28% to 70.98% and agreement from 57.66% to 58.19%.
results.setup: Set 1 = GPT-4-turbo + GPT-3.5-turbo + LLaMA3-8B-Instruct; set 2 = GPT-4-turbo + GPT-3.5-turbo + Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; value is set 1, baseline is set 2
results.table: Table 4, row multi LLMs (set 1), column Position
results.note: Set 2 position consistency 70.98 is the baseline_value.

results.claim: Reasoning judges do not clearly beat GPT-4-turbo on human alignment; gemini-2.0-thinking is best on the human=model2 label (78.31%).
results.setup: LLMEval2 by human label, only valid responses counted; baseline is GPT-4-turbo
results.table: Table 3, row gemini-2.0-thinking, column human=model2 accuracy (%)
results.note: Prose (Sec 4.4.2) prints 78.27% for gemini, 69.44% for GPT-4-turbo model2 and 29.67% for GPT-4-turbo TIE, while Table 3 prints 78.31, 69.47 and 29.73. Table is the primary.

results.claim: All judges are weak on human=TIE labels: GPT-4-turbo 29.73%, o3-mini 42.31%, deepseek r1 17.95%.
results.table: Table 3, row GPT-4-turbo, column human=TIE accuracy (%)
results.note: Prose says GPT-4-turbo outperforms all other models on ties, but Table 3 shows o3-mini 42.31 higher.

results.claim: Authors' empirical recipe for pairwise judging: use a stronger model, swap response positions, and take the majority vote of several rounds.
results.setup: Conclusion of Sec 4.4 experiments with GPT-3.5-turbo base evaluator
results.quote: one is swapping the positions of the evaluation contents, the other is taking the majority voting results from multiple rounds of evaluation, which can effectively mitigate biases

results.claim: GPT-4 tends to favor the first position, ChatGPT the second; in one study Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT under ChatGPT judging just by being placed second.
results.source: Wang et al. 2024, Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators [155]
results.setup: Pairwise judging on Vicuna benchmark queries; no numbers given in the survey
results.quote: GPT-4 tends to favor the first position, while ChatGPT shows a preference for the second position.

results.claim: Judge-cost anecdote: LLM judges correlate strongly with humans on social-cognition tasks (r=0.83) for GPT-4 judges.
results.setup: role-play multi-agent social interactions; details not given
results.quote: GPT-4-based judges correlate strongly with human ratings (r = 0.83) on higher-order social cognition tasks

results.claim: A LLaMA-2 judge reached Cohen's kappa 0.79 checking internal consistency of clinical notes.
Pairwise comparisons beat score-based judging in positional consistency and in LLM-human alignment.
results.source: Liu et al. [95]; Liusie et al. [96]; Zheng et al. [213], as cited
results.quote: Numerous studies have demonstrated that pairwise comparative assessments outperform other judging methods in terms of positional consistency [96, 213].

results.claim: A null model giving a constant irrelevant response can reach high win rates on LLM judges; universal attack phrases inflate scores without improving text.
results.quote: even a "null model" that outputs a constant response irrelevant to input instructions can achieve high win rates for various LLM-as-a-judge methods

limits: The survey's own experiment is small: one run per cell, temperature 0, no CIs or significance tests, judge prompts for the experiment not printed, and only LLMEval2 (agreement) and EvalBiasBench (80 samples, 24 to 34 per bias) are used, so bias cells rest on n=24 to 34.
Sec 4.4.2 prose and Tables 2/3 disagree in a few decimals (78.27 vs 78.31, 69.44 vs 69.47, 29.67 vs 29.73), and prose claims GPT-4-turbo is best on ties while o3-mini scores higher in Table 3.

Explanation hurts and self-validation is useless only for GPT-3.5-turbo as the base evaluator; the survey does not test other base judges and gives causes as speculation ('speculated to be caused by deeper biases').

Agreement was measured with percentage agreement on pairwise labels only; no chance-corrected kappa, no pointwise scoring in the experiment, even though prose says pairwise 'yields more reliable results than pointwise'.

Authors concede current meta-evaluation is insufficient: need a unified benchmark and controlled studies (Sec 4.5), meta-evaluation for large-scale data annotation, and temporal-drift tracking (Sec 6.5).
Table 1 benchmark sizes and bias counts are copied from other work, not measured.
The abstract promises a novel benchmark; the paper's own contribution is the Sec 4.4 meta-evaluation tool and experiment, which reuses LLMEval2 and EvalBiasBench.
practices: Define the evaluation target, how humans evaluate it and gather reliable examples before prompting; then test with cases and retest (Sec 2.5, Fig 8).
Specify scoring dimensions, prefer relative comparison and add examples in the judge prompt (Sec 2.5).
Pick a large model with strong reasoning and instruction following, and run a small-scale meta-evaluation of its bias profile before choosing it (Sec 2.5, Sec 4.4.2).
Force a parseable output format such as \boxed{XX}, a numeric score, or Yes/No, because rule-based token extraction is brittle (Sec 2.3, Sec 2.5).
Use few-shot examples, decompose evaluation steps (G-Eval, DHP) and decompose criteria (BSM, HD-Eval) to cut inter-rater inconsistency (Sec 3.1.1).
Swap the positions of the two responses and average the scores, or mark conflicting verdicts as a tie (PandaLM), to mitigate position bias (Sec 3.1.1).
Convert absolute scoring into pairwise comparison (PARIS) for more stable results (Sec 3.1.1).
Constrain output in structured formats (JSON, form filling 'X: Y') (Sec 3.1.2).
Fine-tune judges on carefully built meta-evaluation data (templates or deep transformation, e.g. OffsetBias with off-topic bad responses) and refine iteratively with feedback (Sec 3.2).
Aggregate multiple rounds or multiple LLM judges by majority vote; avoid mean and best-of-N for pairwise tasks (Sec 3.3.1, Sec 4.4.2).
Use logit-based score smoothing when token probabilities are available, else self-verification (Sec 3.3.2).
Avoid using the same model as evaluator and as the evaluated system, as a stopgap for self-enhancement bias (Sec 4.2.1).
Anonymise model names to avoid compassion-fade bias (Sec 4.2.2).
Do not ask for explanation and verdict in the same call without checking; the survey found it can hurt (Sec 4.4.2).
Report agreement, bias and adversarial robustness as the three meta-evaluation dimensions (Sec 4).

terms.definition: E <- P_LLM(x (+) C): E final evaluation (score, choice, label or sentence), x the input to evaluate, C the context (prompt template and history), (+) the combination operator.
R <- f_R(P_LLM, x, C): an evaluation designed for consistency, robustness and alignment with human judgment, verified by validation, calibration and standardization beyond the basic pipeline.
the tendency of LLM evaluators to favor responses in certain positions within the prompt
how frequently a judge model selects the same response after changing their positions
the extent to which judge models favor a response in certain positions
the percent of disagreement after changing the position of two candidate responses
the tendency to favor responses of a particular length, such as a preference for more verbose responses
LLM evaluators may prefer responses generated by themselves
LLM evaluators favor responses with specific details, including citation of authoritative sources, numerical values, and complex terminologies (also authority bias, citation bias)
preference for a certain text style, e.g. visually appealing content with emojis, or certain emotional tones
the effect of the model names, e.g. higher scores for results labeled gpt-4
bias against certain demographic groups (gender, race, sexual orientation)
evaluators might score expressions from unfamiliar cultures poorly
Task-agnostic biases are inherent to LLMs across applications and depend on foundation-model progress; judgment-specific biases are unique to judging and need targeted optimization.
proportion of samples on which LLM and human annotators agree
the ability of a model to withstand deliberate attempts to manipulate the scores through carefully crafted inputs
judgments drifting over time due to model updates or contextual changes, a type of temporal unreliability
judge classifies responses as win/lose, 'both good tie' or 'both bad tie'
